title: A $15 fee for two weeks
hook: $15 to borrow $100 for two weeks sounds small. What is that per year?

knows: that a loan has a yearly rate (APR)
doesNotKnow: that a small fee on a short loan is a very large yearly rate

misconception: A $15 fee on $100 is a 15% rate.
objective: The learner can explain that the same fee repeats more often on shorter loans, so $15 per $100 for two weeks is $390 per $100 over 26 periods, a simple yearly rate of 390%.

claims.text: A $15 fee on $100 for two weeks is 15% for that period.
A year of 364 days holds 26 two-week periods, so 26 fees of $15 come to $390 per $100, a simple yearly rate of 390%.
claims.source: 364 / 14 = 26; 15 x 26 = 390. Demo.tsx periods(14), yearly(14). The 364-day year is the lesson's simplification (a calendar year is 365 days, 26.07 periods).

claims.text: With the same $15 fee per $100, loans of 7, 28 and 91 days correspond to simple yearly rates of 780%, 195% and 60%.
The fee per loan is the same at every length; the shorter the loan, the more times it repeats in a year.
claims.source: Number of loans in a year = 364 / length in days; the fee is fixed in the model.

claims.text: The lesson is a model: simple annualising with no compounding, the fee only, no rollover, a 364-day year, and no view on any lender.
claims.source: Assumptions of Demo.tsx; stage chip 'Model: simple yearly rate, fee only'.

recall.question: A lender charges $10 to lend $100 for one week. Using 52 weeks in a year, what is the simple yearly rate?
recall.why: The $10 fee repeats 52 times in a year: 10 x 52 = $520 per $100, or 520%. The 10% is the rate for one week only.
